mainTopic: The weight of judging: who may be a judge, how humble and careful he must be, and the rules for running a fair court.
overview: This amud is all about how serious it is to be a judge. It opens by reading the sword-carrying guards around שלמה's bed as judges who fear גיהנם. Two אמוראים then teach that a judge may rule only when the case is as clear as morning, or as certain as the fact that his sister is forbidden to him. רבי יהושע בן לוי teaches that every judge on the court shares the blame for a wrong ruling, even a student sitting before his teacher. That is why רב הונא and רב אשי gathered many people to share the weight. The גמרא then warns against judges who depend on others, judges who are not learned, and judges appointed for money, comparing them to idols and to an אשרה. It shows how רב and מר זוטרא stayed humble when they were honored. Finally it reads פסוקים in שמות and דברים for rules of the courtroom: be patient, prepare the court's tools, never hear one side alone, check before deciding, and treat a litigant as neither friend nor enemy. A story about רב's host begins at the end and continues on the next amud.

steps.title: The guards around שלמה's bed fear the darkness of גיהנם
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק from שיר השירים is brought, and its words 'fear in the nights' are explained as fear of גיהנם, which is dark like night.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'Here is Shlomo's bed, with sixty mighty men around it, from the mighty men of Israel. All of them hold swords and are trained in war, each man with his sword on his thigh, because of fear in the nights.' This means: because of fear of גיהנם, which is like night.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes a teaching that began just before this section by quoting its source פסוק. It explains the phrase 'fear in the nights' as fear of גיהנם.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'fear in the nights' are not read as fear of robbers in the dark. They are read as fear of גיהנם, which is compared to night. This sets the tone for the whole section: judging is serious, and a judge should feel that fear.

keyTerms.meaning: Because of fear in the nights
The place of punishment after death

steps.whyThisMatters: This image of the frightened, sword-ready guard opens the theme for the rest of the section: a judge must feel how heavy his responsibility is.

phrases.english: As it is stated: "Behold, the bed of Solomon;
phrases.notes: שיר השירים 3:7–8

phrases.english: sixty mighty men are around it,
from the mighty men of Israel.
All of them hold the sword, trained in war,
each man with his sword upon his thigh,
because of fear in the nights."
Because of the fear of Gehinnom, which is like the night.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a statement begun before this section by supplying its source פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: That judges should rule with fear of the consequences of a wrong ruling.
steps.raayaSupportSource: שיר השירים 3:7–8, with 'fear in the nights' read as fear of גיהנם.

steps.title: Do courts only judge in the morning?
steps.stepSummary: רבי יאשיה (or רב נחמן בר יצחק) quotes a פסוק telling the house of דוד to judge 'in the morning,' then asks: are courts allowed to judge only in the morning and not the rest of the day?
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יאשיה, and some say רב נחמן בר יצחק, explained: What is the meaning of the פסוק, 'House of David, so says ה׳: Judge justly in the morning, and save the robbed person from the hand of the oppressor'? Do courts judge only in the morning, and not the whole rest of the day?
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching starts with a פסוק that seems to say judging should happen 'in the morning.' The גמרא asks a question to set up the next step: surely courts judge all day long.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Read simply, the פסוק seems to limit judging to the morning. That can't be the point, since courts sit all day. The question shows that 'morning' must mean something else, and the next step explains what.

keyTerms.meaning: He explained a פסוק to bring out its deeper meaning
What is the meaning of what is written?
Is it really so that…? (a question that doubts the plain reading)

phrases.english: Rabbi Yoshiya expounded,
and some say it was Rav Nachman bar Yitzchak:
What is the meaning of that which is written:
"House of David, so says ה׳:
Judge justice in the morning,
phrases.notes: ירמיהו 21:12

phrases.english: and save the robbed from the hand of the oppressor"?
Is it really in the morning that they judge,
and the whole rest of the day they do not judge?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new teaching about how certain a judge must be before ruling, continuing the theme of a judge's fear.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the word 'morning' means in the פסוק, since courts clearly judge all day.

steps.title: Rule only when the case is as clear as morning
steps.stepSummary: 'Morning' means clarity: if the case is as clear to you as the morning light, give your ruling; if not, don't.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, if the matter is as clear to you as the morning, say your ruling. If not, do not say it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question: 'morning' is a picture of clarity. A judge should rule only when the case is that clear to him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'morning' is no longer about the time of day. It now describes how certain the judge must be: as clear as daylight. If he is unsure, he must hold back his ruling.
steps.whatToRemember: A judge should give a ruling only when the case is as clear to him as the morning light.

phrases.english: Rather, if it is clear to you,
the matter, like the morning – say it,
and if not – do not say it.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אִם בָּרוּר לְךָ הַדָּבָר כַּבֹּקֶר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2 by reading 'morning' as a picture of clarity.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: 'Morning' means clarity: rule only when the matter is as clear as morning.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge may rule only when the case is fully clear to him.

steps.title: A second source: wisdom as clear as 'my sister'
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר אבא in the name of רבי יונתן learns the same rule from a פסוק in משלי: rule only when you are as sure as you are that your sister is forbidden to you.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יונתן: We learn it from here: 'Say to wisdom, you are my sister.' If the matter is as clear to you as the fact that your sister is forbidden to you, say it. If not, do not say it.
steps.whatsHappening: A different אמורא brings another פסוק to teach the same rule. It gives a second picture of how sure a judge must be.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule stays the same: don't rule unless you are sure. Only the source and the picture change. Everyone knows for certain that his sister is forbidden to him, and a judge's knowledge should be that firm.

keyTerms.meaning: Say to wisdom: you are my sister

phrases.aramaic: רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן,
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiya bar Abba said that Rabbi Yonatan said:
From here: "Say to wisdom, you are my sister" –
phrases.notes: משלי 7:4

phrases.english: if the matter is clear to you
like your sister, that she is forbidden to you –
say it, and if not – do not say it.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different source for the same rule taught in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: That a judge should rule only when the matter is completely clear.
steps.raayaSupportSource: משלי 7:4, 'Say to wisdom, you are my sister.'
steps.whatToRemember: Two sources, one rule: a judge must be as certain as morning light, or as certain as he is that his sister is forbidden to him.

steps.title: Every judge on the panel shares the responsibility
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי teaches that when ten judges sit together, the 'collar' of responsibility hangs on all of their necks.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהושע בן לוי said: When ten judges sit in judgment, the collar hangs on the neck of every one of them.
steps.whatsHappening: A new teaching: when many judges sit together, each one carries responsibility for the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The 'collar' is a picture of the punishment or blame for a wrong ruling. No judge can hide behind the others, since the responsibility lands on everyone.

keyTerms.meaning: A collar; here, the responsibility for the ruling

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
Ten who sit in judgment –
the collar hangs on the neck of all of them.
phrases.notes: A קולר is the iron collar put on a prisoner; here it stands for the blame for a wrong ruling.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from how sure a judge must be to who carries the responsibility on a panel of judges.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Every judge on a court shares responsibility for its ruling.

steps.title: Isn't that obvious?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why רבי יהושע בן לוי needed to say this, since it seems obvious that every judge is responsible.
steps.simpleTranslation: That is obvious!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the teaching: of course every judge who sits on the case is responsible. This sets up the next step, which shows what the teaching adds.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא assumes a teacher would not bother to say something everyone already knows. So it asks what new point רבי יהושע בן לוי is making.

phrases.english: It is obvious!

steps.triggerLanguage: פְּשִׁיטָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the need for the teaching in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יהושע בן לוי's statement that all ten judges share responsibility.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Judges who rule together are obviously all responsible, so the statement seems to teach nothing new.

steps.title: Even a student sitting before his teacher is responsible
steps.stepSummary: The teaching is needed for a student sitting in front of his teacher: even he shares the responsibility.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is needed only for a student sitting before his teacher.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers: the new point is that even a student sitting before his teacher shares the responsibility.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might think a student is not responsible, since his teacher is the one in charge. רבי יהושע בן לוי teaches that the student is also included under the 'collar.'

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for… (shows the new point)

steps.confusionAlert: The teaching was not about ordinary judges, who are obviously responsible. Its real point is the student sitting before his teacher, who you might have thought was free of responsibility.

phrases.english: It is needed only
for a student who sits before his teacher.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא צְרִיכָא אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 6 by naming the case where the teaching adds something new.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the teaching to a specific case (לא צריכא).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A student sitting before his teacher might not share responsibility, since the teacher leads.
steps.terutzMaskana: Even that student carries part of the responsibility for the ruling.
steps.whatToRemember: Everyone sitting on the court, even a student before his teacher, shares the responsibility for the ruling.

steps.title: רב הונא gathers ten scholars for every case
steps.stepSummary: Whenever a case came to רב הונא, he gathered ten רבנן from the study hall so that each would carry only a small share of the responsibility.
steps.simpleTranslation: When a case came before רב הונא, he would gather and bring ten רבנן from the study hall. He said: So that only a splinter from the beam will reach us.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells how רב הונא acted on the idea that responsibility is shared. He brought in many scholars so the weight would be spread out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since all the judges share the 'collar,' more judges means each one carries less. The full responsibility is like a big beam, and each person ends up with just a splinter of it.

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא, כִּי הֲוָה אָתֵי דִּינָא לְקַמֵּיהּ,
phrases.english: Rav Huna, when a case would come before him,
would gather and bring
ten rabbis from the study hall.
He said: So that
only a splinter from the beam will reach us.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא כִּי הֲוָה אָתֵי דִּינָא לְקַמֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows an אמורא acting on the idea from step 5 that judges share responsibility.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Bringing many judges onto a case spreads the responsibility, so each carries only a small part.

steps.title: רב אשי gathers all the butchers for a טריפה question
steps.stepSummary: Whenever a טריפה question came to רב אשי, he gathered all the butchers of מתא מחסיא, for the same reason: so each would carry only a splinter of the responsibility.
steps.simpleTranslation: When a טריפה question came before רב אשי, he would gather and bring all the butchers of מתא מחסיא. He said: So that only a splinter from the beam will reach us.
steps.whatsHappening: A second story with the same lesson, this time about a question of איסור והיתר instead of a court case. רב אשי brought in all the local butchers to share the weight of the ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idea of sharing responsibility is not limited to court cases. It also applies when a רב rules on whether meat is טריפה. רב אשי gives the same reason as רב הונא: each person ends up carrying only a splinter of the beam.

keyTerms.meaning: A טריפה question (whether an animal is forbidden because of a fatal defect)
The town where רב אשי lived and taught

steps.whatToRemember: Great רבנן spread the weight of a ruling by bringing in others, whether judges for a court case or butchers for a טריפה question, so each carried only a 'splinter from the beam.'

phrases.english: Rav Ashi, when there would come
a treifa question before him,
phrases.notes: Someone brought meat and asked if the animal had a defect that makes it forbidden.

phrases.english: would gather and bring
all the butchers of Mata Mechasya.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר: כִּי הֵיכִי דְּלִימְטְיַין שִׁיבָּא מִכְּשׁוּרָא.
phrases.english: He said: So that only a splinter from the beam will reach us.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי כִּי הֲוָה אָתֵי טְרֵיפְתָּא לְקַמֵּיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A parallel story to step 8, carrying the same idea over from court cases to טריפה questions.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even for איסור והיתר questions, a רב may bring in others to share the responsibility of the ruling.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Ruling is a heavy responsibility, and spreading it among many people lightens the share each one carries.

steps.title: A judge must be independent like a king
steps.stepSummary: רב דימי reports a דרשה of רב נחמן בר כהן: a judge who needs nothing from anyone strengthens the land, but a judge who depends on others, like a כהן collecting gifts, destroys it.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב דימי came, he said: רב נחמן בר כהן explained the פסוק 'A king with justice makes the land stand, but a man of gifts tears it down.' If a judge is like a king, who needs nothing from anyone, he makes the land stand. If he is like a כהן who goes around the threshing floors asking for gifts, he tears it down.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about what kind of person should be a judge: someone who does not depend on others.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק contrasts a 'king' with a 'man of תרומות'. רב נחמן בר כהן reads these as two types of judges. A judge who needs favors from people may be pulled to favor them, while an independent judge can rule honestly.

keyTerms.meaning: Expounded, explained a פסוק to teach a lesson
Gifts given to a כהן from the crops
The threshing floors, where grain was processed and תרומה was handed out

steps.whyThisMatters: This opens a new theme in the sugya: not only do judges carry responsibility, they must also be the kind of people who can judge without being influenced.

phrases.english: When Rav Dimi came, he said:
Rav Nachman bar Kohen expounded:
What is the meaning of that which is written:
"The king by justice establishes the land,
phrases.notes: משלי 29:4

phrases.english: but a man of gifts overthrows it"?
If a judge is like a king,
who does not need anything, he establishes the land;
but if he is like a kohen
who goes around the threshing floors, he overthrows it.
phrases.notes: Picture a כהן going from farm to farm asking for his gifts. He depends on everyone's goodwill.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי אֲתָא רַב דִּימִי אָמַר: דָּרַשׁ רַב נַחְמָן בַּר כֹּהֵן, מַאי דִּכְתִיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the shared responsibility of judges to the required character of a judge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge who is independent and needs nothing from others strengthens society; a judge who depends on others' gifts damages it.

steps.title: An unlearned judge has nothing to say
steps.stepSummary: The house of the נשיא appointed an unlearned judge. He asked יהודה בר נחמני to serve as his interpreter, but when the interpreter leaned in to hear, the judge said nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: The house of the נשיא appointed a judge who was not learned. He told יהודה בר נחמני, the interpreter of ריש לקיש: 'Stand next to me as my interpreter.' יהודה stood and leaned over to hear him, but the judge said nothing at all.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story about a judge who was appointed without being a scholar. This step sets up the story, and the next step gives the interpreter's sharp response.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In a public lecture, the scholar would quietly say his words and the interpreter would announce them to the crowd. Here the interpreter leaned in, ready to repeat, and the judge had no Torah to give. The silence shows that the appointment was empty.

keyTerms.meaning: The house of the נשיא, the leadership that appointed judges
Interpreter who announced a scholar's lecture to the audience
Here: the one who stands and repeats the lecture aloud

phrases.english: The house of the Nasi
appointed a judge who was not learned.
He said to Yehuda bar Nachmani,
the interpreter of Reish Lakish:
"Stand over me as an interpreter."
phrases.notes: The word עֲלֵיהּ literally means 'over him'. It is a polite way of saying 'over me'.

phrases.english: He stood up and bent over him,
and the judge did not say anything to him at all.

steps.triggerLanguage: דְּבֵי נְשִׂיאָה אוֹקְמוּ דַּיָּינָא דְּלָא הֲוָה גְּמִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows in a real story what happens when an unqualified judge is appointed.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A story showing that an unlearned judge had no Torah to offer once he was put in front of the public.

steps.title: The interpreter compares the judge to a silent idol
steps.stepSummary: יהודה בר נחמני opens with a פסוק about a gold-covered wood or stone idol that cannot speak, and warns that הקב"ה will punish those who appoint such judges.
steps.simpleTranslation: The interpreter began and said: 'Woe to the one who says to wood, Wake up! and to a silent stone, Get up! Can it teach? It is covered with gold and silver, but there is no spirit in it at all.' And הקב"ה will one day punish those who appoint such judges, as it says: 'And ה׳ is in His holy Sanctuary; let all the earth be silent before Him.'
steps.whatsHappening: This is the climax of the story: the interpreter uses a פסוק to publicly point out that the judge is like an empty idol, and warns the people who appointed him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The idol in the פסוק is covered in gold and silver but has no life inside, just like a judge who was appointed for money but has no Torah inside. The next פסוק says ה׳ sits in His Sanctuary over all the earth, meaning He will judge those who made this appointment.

keyTerms.meaning: To punish, to collect payment for a wrong

steps.whatToRemember: An unqualified judge is like a shiny idol: impressive on the outside, empty on the inside. Responsibility falls on those who appointed him.

phrases.english: He opened and said:
phrases.notes: The speaker here is the interpreter, יהודה בר נחמני, filling the silence himself.

phrases.english: "Woe to him who says to the wood: Awake,
Arise, to the silent stone;
can it teach?
Behold, it is overlaid with gold and silver,
and there is no breath at all within it."
phrases.notes: חבקוק 2:19

phrases.english: And in the future the Holy One, Blessed be He,
will punish those who appoint them,
as it is said:
"And ה׳ is in His holy Sanctuary;
let all the earth be silent before Him."
phrases.notes: חבקוק 2:20, the very next פסוק.

steps.triggerLanguage: פָּתַח וְאָמַר: ״הוֹי אוֹמֵר לָעֵץ הָקִיצָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the interpreter's response to the judge's silence in the story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Those who appoint an unlearned judge will be punished by הקב"ה.

steps.title: Appointing an unfit judge is like planting an אשרה
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש teaches that appointing an unfit judge is like planting an אשרה, learned from the closeness of the פסוק about judges to the פסוק forbidding an אשרה.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: Anyone who appoints an unfit judge over the community is as if he planted an אשרה among Israel. As it says, 'Judges and officers you shall appoint for yourself,' and right near it, 'You shall not plant for yourself an אשרה, any tree.'
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש gives a strong general rule about appointing unfit judges, and brings a source for it from the order of the פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof is from סמיכות, the fact that two topics are placed near each other in the Torah. Because the פסוק about appointing judges sits right near the ban on planting an אשרה, the Torah is hinting that a bad judge is like an idol planted in the community.

keyTerms.meaning: A tree planted for idol worship
Next to it, placed close by in the Torah
Officers who enforce the judges' rulings

steps.confusionAlert: ריש לקיש is not saying an unfit judge is literally עבודה זרה. He is making a comparison: the damage and seriousness are like planting an אשרה.

phrases.english: Reish Lakish said:
Anyone who appoints a judge over the community
who is not fit,
it is as if he plants an ashera among Israel,
as it is said: "Judges and officers you shall appoint for yourself,"
phrases.notes: דברים 16:18

phrases.english: and next to it is written:
"You shall not plant for yourself an ashera, any kind of tree."
phrases.notes: דברים 16:21

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ: כׇּל הַמַּעֲמִיד דַּיָּין עַל הַצִּיבּוּר שֶׁאֵינוֹ הָגוּן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of the story with a general rule from ריש לקיש, whose own interpreter was in the story.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Appointing an unfit judge over the community is comparable to planting an אשרה in Israel.

steps.title: Even worse where scholars are available
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי adds that if תלמידי חכמים are available and an unfit judge is appointed anyway, it is like planting the אשרה next to the מזבח.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: And in a place where there are תלמידי חכמים, it is as if he planted it next to the מזבח, as it says: 'beside the altar of ה׳ your God.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי builds on ריש לקיש's teaching and adds a more serious case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same פסוק about the אשרה continues 'beside the altar of ה׳ your God.' רב אשי reads this as the case where worthy scholars were available and passed over. Choosing an unfit judge then is like placing an idol right by the holiest place.
steps.whatToRemember: Appointing an unfit judge is like planting an אשרה; doing it when real scholars are available is like planting it right next to the מזבח.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that the community has a real duty to pick the most fitting judges it has. The next steps keep going with the theme of unfit judges, this time ones appointed for money.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
And in a place where there are Torah scholars,
it is as if he planted it next to the altar,
as it is said: "beside the altar of ה׳ your God."
phrases.notes: This is the end of the same פסוק ריש לקיש quoted, דברים 16:21.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: וּבִמְקוֹם שֶׁיֵּשׁ תַּלְמִידֵי חֲכָמִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a more severe level to ריש לקיש's comparison, using the rest of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Appointing an unfit judge where תלמידי חכמים are available is like planting an אשרה next to the מזבח.

steps.title: Is it only silver and gold idols that are forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes 'Do not make with Me gods of silver and gods of gold' and asks: does that mean gods of wood are allowed?
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: 'Do not make with Me gods of silver and gods of gold.' Does that mean only silver and gold gods are forbidden, and wooden ones are allowed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes a פסוק and points out a problem with its plain meaning. This sets up the next step, where רב אשי will give a new reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Every kind of idol is forbidden, so why does the פסוק name only silver and gold? The question forces us to look for a different meaning of the פסוק. Since the theme here is judges, the answer will connect it to them.

phrases.english: It is written: "You shall not make with Me
gods of silver and gods of gold."
phrases.notes: שמות 20:20

phrases.english: Gods of silver and gods of gold
are what one may not make,
but ones of wood are permitted?

steps.triggerLanguage: הָא דְּעֵץ שְׁרֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the theme of unfit judges compared to idols (steps 12-14) by bringing a new פסוק that seems to be about idols.
steps.kashyaTarget: The plain reading of the פסוק 'gods of silver and gods of gold'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If only silver and gold idols are named, it would imply wooden idols are allowed, which cannot be true.

steps.title: The פסוק is about judges who buy their position
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי explains that the פסוק means a judge who got his post because of silver or gold.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: It means a 'god' (a judge) who comes because of silver, and a 'god' who comes because of gold.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי answers the question: the פסוק is not about idols at all, but about judges appointed because they paid money.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word אלהים can also mean judges. So 'gods of silver and gold' means judges who got their job through silver and gold. That explains why wood is not mentioned: the point is the money paid for the appointment, not the material of an idol.

keyTerms.meaning: here: a judge (the תורה sometimes calls judges אֱלֹהִים)

steps.confusionAlert: Don't read this as a new rule about idols. רב אשי is saying the whole פסוק is really about judges appointed through money.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:
A "god" who comes because of silver,
phrases.notes: Here "god" means a judge, who got his position by paying.

phrases.english: and a "god" who comes because of gold.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב אָשֵׁי: אֱלוֹהַּ הַבָּא בִּשְׁבִיל כֶּסֶף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 15 by reading the פסוק as being about judges.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק is about idols, which would wrongly imply wooden idols are allowed.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק is about judges appointed through silver or gold, so there is no implication about wood.

steps.title: What רב said on his way to court
steps.stepSummary: רב reminded himself that a judge risks punishment, earns nothing, and should only hope to come home as free of sin as he left.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב went to court, he would say: By his own choice he goes out toward death, he does not take care of his household's needs, and he comes home empty-handed. If only my coming home would be just like my leaving.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells how רב kept himself humble and careful each time he went to judge.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב points out three things: judging wrongly can bring punishment from Heaven, it takes time away from earning a living, and a judge takes no pay. His only wish is to come home without having sinned. This is the opposite of the judge who seeks the post for money in step 16.

phrases.aramaic: רַב, כִּי הֲוָה אָתֵי לְבֵי דִּינָא,
phrases.english: Rav, when he would come to the court,
would say this:
By his own will he goes out to death,
phrases.notes: רב is talking about himself. A judge who rules wrongly can be punished by Heaven.

phrases.english: and the needs of his house he does not take care of,
and he enters his house empty-handed.
If only the coming in would be like the going out.
phrases.notes: He means: may I come home just as free of sin as when I left.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב, כִּי הֲוָה אָתֵי לְבֵי דִּינָא, אָמַר הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from unfit judges to the humble attitude of a great judge.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge should see judging as a serious risk with no personal gain, and hope only to finish without sin.

steps.title: רב humbles himself when a crowd follows him
steps.stepSummary: When רב saw a crowd of scholars following him, he quoted a פסוק from איוב about how even the greatest person ends up lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב saw a crowd of scholars walking behind him, he said: 'Though his greatness rises to the heavens... he will be lost forever like his own dung.'
steps.whatsHappening: Another story of רב's humility: when people honored him, he reminded himself how temporary human greatness is.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Honor can make a judge proud. רב used a harsh פסוק to push away that pride the moment it could start. This continues the picture of the right attitude for a judge.

phrases.english: When he would see
a crowd of scholars behind him,
he said: "Though his greatness rises up to the heavens, etc.,
like his own dung he will be lost forever, etc."
phrases.notes: איוב 20:6-7

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי הָוֵי חָזֵי אַמְבּוּהָא דְסָפְרֵי אַבָּתְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second humility practice of רב, continuing step 17.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When honored, a leader should remind himself that human greatness does not last.

steps.title: מר זוטרא חסידא humbles himself when carried in honor
steps.stepSummary: When people carried מר זוטרא on their shoulders on the שבת of the festival, he quoted a פסוק that power and crowns do not last forever.
steps.simpleTranslation: מר זוטרא the pious, when they carried him on their shoulders on the שבת of the festival, would say: 'For strength is not forever, and does a crown last for all generations?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a similar story about another great sage, מר זוטרא חסידא, who also guarded himself against pride.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being carried on people's shoulders is a very big honor. מר זוטרא answered it with a פסוק saying that power and honor are temporary. Together with רב, this shows a pattern: great leaders actively fight pride.
steps.whatToRemember: רב and מר זוטרא both used פסוקים to fight pride when people honored them. A true judge or leader must stay humble.

phrases.english: Mar Zutra the Pious,
when they would carry him on their shoulders
on the Shabbos of the festival,
would say this:
"For strength is not forever,
and does a crown last for all generations?"
phrases.notes: משלי 27:24

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר זוּטְרָא חֲסִידָא, כִּי הֲווֹ מְכַתְּפִי לֵיהּ בְּשַׁבְּתָא דְרִיגְלָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Parallel humility story from a different sage, closing the section on humility.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Power and honor are temporary; a leader must remember this when he is honored.

steps.title: The source for 'be patient in judgment'
steps.stepSummary: בר קפרא learns the rule 'be patient in judgment' from the fact that 'Do not go up by steps' sits right next to 'And these are the laws.'
steps.simpleTranslation: בר קפרא taught: Where do we learn what the רבנן said, 'Be patient in judgment'? From the פסוק 'Do not go up by steps,' and right next to it is 'And these are the laws.'
steps.whatsHappening: בר קפרא finds a source in the תורה for the famous teaching that judges must not rush.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The מזבח was climbed by a ramp, not steps, so one would not take big hurried strides. Because the next פסוק begins the laws of judging, בר קפרא applies the same idea to judges: go slowly and carefully. The tool here is סמיכות, learning from two פסוקים placed next to each other.

keyTerms.meaning: and placed right next to it

steps.whyThisMatters: This gives a תורה source for the very first teaching of the אנשי כנסת הגדולה in אבות, that judges must take their time.

phrases.english: Bar Kappara expounded:
From where is this thing that the Rabbis said,
"Be patient in judgment"?
phrases.notes: This is the opening teaching of אבות 1:1.

phrases.english: As it is written: "Do not go up by steps,"
phrases.notes: שמות 20:23, about going up to the מזבח.

phrases.english: and next to it: "And these are the laws."
phrases.notes: שמות 21:1

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּרֵשׁ בַּר קַפָּרָא: מְנָא הָא מִילְּתָא דַּאֲמַרוּ רַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from stories of humility to a תורה source for how a judge must act.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Judges must be patient in judgment, learned from the closeness of 'Do not go up by steps' to 'And these are the laws.'

steps.title: A judge may not step over the heads of the people
steps.stepSummary: רבי אליעזר uses the same two פסוקים to teach that a judge must not walk over people sitting on the floor.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אליעזר said: Where do we learn that a judge should not step over the heads of the holy nation? From 'Do not go up by steps,' and right next to it, 'And these are the laws.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אליעזר learns a different lesson for judges from the very same pair of פסוקים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: People sat on the floor at a lecture, and a judge walking through them would look like he was stepping on their heads. Just as one may not climb proudly to the מזבח, a judge may not climb over the people. Same source as step 20, but a different rule: respect for the people instead of patience in judging.
steps.confusionAlert: Steps 20 and 21 quote the exact same פסוקים, but they teach two different rules. Don't merge them.
steps.whatToRemember: The פסוק 'Do not go up by steps,' placed next to 'And these are the laws,' teaches judges two things: judge patiently, and don't step over the people.

phrases.english: Rabbi Eliezer said:
From where do we know that a judge

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁלֹּא יְפַסֵּעַ עַל רָאשֵׁי עַם קוֹדֶשׁ?
phrases.english: should not step over the heads of the holy nation?
As it says: "Do not go up by steps,"
and next to it: "And these are the laws."

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֱלִיעֶזֶר: מִנַּיִין לְדַיָּין שֶׁלֹּא יְפַסֵּעַ עַל רָאשֵׁי עַם קוֹדֶשׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same סמיכות as step 20 to learn a different rule for judges.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge may not step over the heads of the people, learned from the closeness of 'Do not go up by steps' to 'And these are the laws.'

steps.title: Why does the פסוק say 'set' instead of 'teach'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the פסוק says ״אשר תשים״ ("that you shall set") when ״אשר תלמדם״ ("that you shall teach them") would seem more natural.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says "that you shall set before them." It should have said "that you shall teach them"!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the פסוק ״ואלה המשפטים״ and asks about one word in it. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Laws are normally "taught," so the word "set" looks odd. The גמרא assumes the תורה chose this word on purpose to add something more than teaching.

keyTerms.meaning: "That you shall set", the words in the פסוק being asked about
"That you shall teach them", the wording the גמרא expected
"It should have said", a way of pointing out unexpected wording

phrases.english: "That you shall set"?
phrases.notes: שמות 21:1, the same פסוק used in the last two steps.

phrases.english: It should have said "that you shall teach them"!

steps.triggerLanguage: ״אֲשֶׁר תְּלַמְּדֵם״ מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Keeps working on the same פסוק (״ואלה המשפטים״) that steps 20-21 used, now looking at its next words.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What extra lesson comes from the word "set" instead of "teach"?

steps.title: 'Set' refers to the judges' tools
steps.stepSummary: רבי ירמיה (or רבי חייא בר אבא) answers that "set before them" means the judges' tools must be placed ready.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ירמיה said, and some say it was רבי חייא בר אבא: These are the judges' tools.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. "Setting" something before people means putting physical things in place: the tools a בית דין needs.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Teaching is only words, but setting means actual objects. So the פסוק hints that a court must have the tools to carry out its rulings, not just know the law.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yirmeya said,
and some say Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba:
These are the judges' tools.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יִרְמְיָה, וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 22.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: "Set" means the judges' tools must be placed and ready.

steps.title: רב הונא calls for the tools of his 'shop'
steps.stepSummary: Before going to judge, רב הונא would ask for his "shop tools": a rod and strap, a שופר, and a sandal.
steps.simpleTranslation: When רב הונא went out to judge, he would say: Bring me the tools of my shop: a rod and a strap, a שופר, and a sandal.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that shows the judges' tools from the last step in real life.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב הונא lists the actual tools: the rod and strap for מלקות, the שופר for נידוי, and the sandal for חליצה. Calling them "shop tools" shows he saw judging as real work that needs real equipment.

keyTerms.meaning: A rod and a strap, used for מלקות

phrases.aramaic: רַב הוּנָא, כִּי הֲוָה נָפֵק לְדִינָא,
phrases.english: Rav Huna, when he would go out to judge,
would say this:
Bring out for me the tools of my shop:
a rod and a strap,
and a shofar, and a sandal.
phrases.notes: The שופר was used when putting someone in נידוי, and the sandal for חליצה.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב הוּנָא, כִּי הֲוָה נָפֵק לְדִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows the judges' tools of step 23 being used in practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge prepares the tools of the court before he sits to judge.

steps.title: Be careful with punishment
steps.stepSummary: From ״ואצוה את שופטיכם״, רבי יוחנן learns that משה told the judges to be careful when it comes to the rod and strap.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And I commanded your judges at that time." רבי יוחנן said: When it comes to the rod and the strap, be careful.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new פסוק in דברים about judges. רבי יוחנן reads "I commanded" as a special warning about punishments.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A "command" means urging someone to act carefully. Since the rod and strap were just mentioned, רבי יוחנן says the command was about punishment: a judge must act with care and alertness when he punishes someone.

keyTerms.meaning: Careful, alert and quick to act

phrases.english: "And I commanded your judges at that time."
phrases.notes: דברים 1:16

phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said:
Regarding the rod and the strap, be careful.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וָאֲצַוֶּה אֶת שֹׁפְטֵיכֶם בָּעֵת הַהִיא״. אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves to a new פסוק but links to the rod and strap of step 24.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge must be careful when giving punishment.

steps.title: Do not hear one side without the other
steps.stepSummary: רבי חנינא learns from ״שמוע בין אחיכם״ that a judge may not hear one בעל דין before the other arrives, and a בעל דין may not present his side early either.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Hear between your brothers and judge." רבי חנינא said: This warns the judge not to hear one side's words before the other side comes. It also warns a בעל דין not to explain his words to the judge before the other side comes. Read it also as "make heard between your brothers."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי חנינא learns two warnings from the next words of the פסוק: one for the judge and one for the people in the case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Hear between your brothers" means hear both of them together. The warning for the judge is in the plain word ״שמוע". The warning for the בעל דין comes from reading the same letters as ״שַׁמַּע", "make heard," which speaks to the person presenting his case.

keyTerms.meaning: One side in a court case
The other side in the case
"Read it as", reading the same word with different vowels

steps.whyThisMatters: This is the source that a judge may not hear one side of a case alone, and a person may not present his case to the judge when the other side is not there.

phrases.english: "Hear between your brothers and judge":
Rabbi Chanina said:
It is a warning to the judge not to hear
the words of one side
before the other side comes,
and a warning to a person in the case
not to explain his words to the judge
before the other side comes.
Read it also as: "Make heard between your brothers."
phrases.notes: Same letters, different vowels. "Make heard" speaks to the person telling his side, so he is warned too.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״שָׁמֹעַ בֵּין אֲחֵיכֶם וּשְׁפַטְתֶּם״ – אָמַר רַבִּי חֲנִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues reading the same פסוק from דברים, moving to its next words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Neither the judge nor a בעל דין may let one side be heard without the other side present.

steps.title: A different source for the בעל דין's warning
steps.stepSummary: רב כהנא learns the בעל דין's warning from ״לא תשא״, read as ״לא תשיא".
steps.simpleTranslation: רב כהנא said: The source is from here: from "Do not accept" read as "do not cause someone else to accept."
steps.whatsHappening: רב כהנא gives a different source for the warning to the בעל דין, instead of רבי חנינא's "make heard."
steps.deeperAnalysis: ״לא תשא שמע שוא" plainly tells the judge not to accept a false report. By reading it as ״לא תשיא", רב כהנא also makes it speak to the person who would cause the judge to accept it: the בעל דין who presents his side alone.

keyTerms.meaning: "Do not cause someone else to accept"

phrases.english: Rav Kahana said: From here,
from "do not accept": read it as "do not cause to accept."
phrases.notes: שמות 23:1, ״לא תשא שמע שוא״. He reads the same letters with different vowels.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב כָּהֲנָא אָמַר: מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a different source for the second warning of step 26.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The בעל דין's warning comes from ״לא תשא" read as ״לא תשיא".

steps.title: Check the case first, then decide
steps.stepSummary: From ״ושפטתם צדק״, ריש לקיש teaches that a judge must first make sure the judgment is right and only then decide it.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And judge with righteousness." ריש לקיש said: Make sure the judgment is right, and after that decide it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to the פסוק in דברים and reads its next words. ריש לקיש explains what "judge righteously" requires.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Righteous" judging is not just meaning well. The judge must first look into every detail of the case until he is sure, and only then give a final ruling.

keyTerms.meaning: Make sure the judgment is correct

phrases.english: "And judge with righteousness."
Reish Lakish said:

phrases.aramaic: צַדֵּק אֶת הַדִּין, וְאַחַר כָּךְ חׇתְכֵהוּ.
phrases.english: Make sure the judgment is right, and after that decide it.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וּשְׁפַטְתֶּם צֶדֶק״. אָמַר רֵישׁ לָקִישׁ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Returns to the פסוק from דברים after רב כהנא's side point.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge must check a case fully before deciding it.

steps.title: Fair even between a house and its upper floor
steps.stepSummary: From ״בין איש ובין אחיו ובין גרו״, רב יהודה teaches that a judge must be careful even when dividing a house from its upper floor.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Between a man and his brother and his stranger." רב יהודה said: Even between a house and an upper floor.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reads the next words of the פסוק. רב יהודה teaches that a judge must be fair even in small differences.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "Between a man and his brother" points to brothers dividing what they own. רב יהודה says the judge must weigh even the difference in value between the ground floor and the upper floor, so neither brother gets less than his share.

keyTerms.meaning: "His stranger", the גר living with him
A house and its upper floor

steps.whatToRemember: The פסוק in דברים teaches a whole set of rules for judges: be careful with punishment (רבי יוחנן), never hear one side alone (רבי חנינא, רב כהנא), check before deciding (ריש לקיש), and be fair even in small details (רב יהודה, here and in the next step).

phrases.english: "Between a man and his brother and his stranger."
Rav Yehuda said:
Even between a house and an upper floor.
phrases.notes: He means brothers dividing a building: the judge must weigh even which floor is worth more.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״בֵּין אִישׁ וּבֵין אָחִיו וּבֵין גֵּרוֹ״. אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues to the last words of the same פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge must be exact even about small differences in value, like a house versus its upper floor.

steps.title: Being careful even between an oven and a stove
steps.stepSummary: On the words ״ובין גרו״, רב יהודה teaches that a judge must be careful even when dividing an oven from a stove.
steps.simpleTranslation: "And his stranger": רב יהודה said, even between an oven and a stove.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next words of the same פסוק, ״ובין גרו״, and רב יהודה learns that a judge must judge carefully even in tiny divisions, like an oven and a stove.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the last step, רב יהודה learned from ״בין איש ובין אחיו״ that a judge must be careful even when dividing a house from its upper floor. Here he goes smaller still: even two household items standing side by side must be divided fairly. No case is too small to deserve full care.

keyTerms.meaning: His stranger, or the one living with him (from גּוּר, to dwell)

phrases.english: "And between his stranger."
phrases.notes: Same פסוק as before (דברים 1:16). גרו sounds like גור, to dwell, so it hints at things that sit together in a home.

phrases.english: Rav Yehuda said:
Even between an oven and a stove.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״וּבֵין גֵּרוֹ״. אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues רב יהודה's reading of the same פסוק, moving from house and upper floor to oven and stove.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge must be careful even when dividing an oven from a stove.

steps.title: Do not treat a litigant as someone you know
steps.stepSummary: On ״לא תכירו פנים במשפט״, רבי יהודה reads it as 'do not recognize him': a judge must not act as the litigant's friend.
steps.simpleTranslation: "Do not recognize faces in judgment": רבי יהודה says, do not recognize him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to the next פסוק, and רבי יהודה explains it to mean that a judge must not treat a litigant as a friend or acquaintance.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word תכירו means 'recognize.' רבי יהודה says the judge must not 'recognize' the litigant, meaning he should not let a friendship lean him toward that side. In court, the judge acts as if he does not know him.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not recognize faces, do not show favor
Do not recognize him (do not treat him as a friend)

phrases.english: "You shall not recognize faces in judgment."
phrases.notes: דברים 1:17

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says: Do not recognize him.

steps.triggerLanguage: ״לֹא תַכִּירוּ פָנִים בַּמִּשְׁפָּט״. רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from ״ובין גרו״ to the next פסוק in משה's charge to the judges.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge must not favor a litigant because he knows him.

steps.title: Do not treat a litigant as a stranger or enemy
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר reads the same פסוק as 'do not make him a stranger': a judge must not act coldly against a litigant either.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר says: do not estrange him.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר gives a second reading of the same פסוק, warning the judge not to treat a litigant as an enemy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יהודה warned against leaning toward someone you like. רבי אלעזר warns about the opposite danger: pushing someone away because you dislike him. Together they show that a judge must stand exactly in the middle, neither friend nor enemy.

keyTerms.meaning: Do not make him a stranger (do not treat him as an enemy)
A stranger, the root behind תנכרהו

steps.whatToRemember: A judge must not act like the litigant's friend (רבי יהודה) and must not act like his enemy (רבי אלעזר).

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar says: Do not estrange him.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אוֹמֵר: לֹא תְּנַכְּרֵהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, opposite-direction reading of the same פסוק that רבי יהודה explained.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A judge must not treat a litigant as an enemy or stranger.

steps.title: רב's host comes to him for a court case
steps.stepSummary: A story begins: רב's host comes before רב with a court case, and רב first asks if he is his host.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב's host came before him for a judgment. רב said to him: Are you not my host? He said: Yes. He said: I have a court case. רב said to him:
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a story that shows the rule about not favoring someone you know. This step sets up the scene, and רב's answer comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A host who gave רב a place to stay is exactly the kind of person a judge might favor. רב first makes sure he really is his host, and the man then says he has a case to be judged. The story stops right before רב replies, so the point of the story is still coming.

keyTerms.meaning: A host, someone who gives a guest a place to stay
For a judgment, for a court case
I have a case to be judged

phrases.english: Rav's host
came before him for a judgment.
He said to him: Are you not my host?
He said to him: Yes.
He said to him: I have a case to be judged.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a story that puts the rule against favoring a familiar litigant into practice.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Setup only: רב's host, whom a judge might favor, brings a case before רב. רב's response follows.
